speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
WThen I was in committee before with my estimates I told the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) that when my estimates came up again I would give him a statement of the number of appointments made in the Department of Marine and Fisheries under section 21 of the Civil Service Act. This is the statement :-
Captain Louis Arthur Demers, wreck commissioner, aged 55, was appointed on the 2nd of May, 1916, at a salary of $3,300 per annum. His present salary is $3,400 per annum. He entered the outside service of the department on the 11th of October, 1904, after having served some twelve years with fishery cruisers; he was transferred to the inside service on 1st September, 1908,

and appointed wreck commissioner on the 1st August, 1910. He resigned to 'become harbour master at Montreal on the 1st June, 1912. When Captain Lindsay, his successor as wreck commissioner, was placed in charge of the Montreal and Quebec pilotage the office of wreck commissioner became vacant, and an view of Captain Demers' special qualifications for the position he was reappointed thereto.
Mr. Thomas Robert Ferguson, chairman of the Board of Steamship Inspection, entered the outside service of the department in May, 1889. On the superannuation of Chairman Edward Adams, the officer who, by length of service, efficiency and technical qualifications, was entitled to succeed him, was Mr. Ferguson, who was at that time inspector of Government steamships at Quebec, and the department so recommended. Mr. Ferguson is 51 years of age. The date of his appointment as chairman of the 'board is 8th May, 1913; salary on appointment, $2,800 per annum; present .salary, $3,200 per annum.
Mr. George Herbert Flood, aged 56, was appointed purchasing and contract agent 1st December, 1915, at a salary of $3,300 per annum. His present salary is $3,500 per annum. Prior to his appointment as purchasing and contract agent Mr. Flood had been the agent of the department at St. John, N.B., since November, 1909. On the resignation of Mr. Cecil Doutre as purchasing and contract agent, the department considered Mr. Flood's experience as agent at St. John, and also as a former business man, specially fitted him for the vacant position, and, after the issue of a certificate of qualification by the Civil Service Commission, the department recommended him for the position of purchasing and contract agent.
Mr. Hope Vere Anderson, aged 27, was transferred from the Department of Mines to the Department of Marine by Order in Council on the 5th September, 1913; salary on appointment $1,600 per annum, present salary $1,750. The services of a mechanical engineer were required iij. the chief engineer's branch of the department, and the Civil Service Commissioners recommended Mr. Anderson for the position; he was accordingly appointed.
Mr. Arnt Christian Andresen, aged 32, was appointed by Order in Council of the 18th May, 1914, to the chief engineer's branch of the department at a salary of $1,200 per annum; he now receives $1,250 per annum. He is at present in a Canadian Battalion on overseas service in France.

His appointment was recommended by the Civil Service Commissioners in response to an application for a clerk with the special qualifications above mentioned.
Mr. Joseph Henry Vaughan, aged 39, has been in the service of the department since June, 1908. His salary on appointment to his present position was $1,600 per annum. He has not yet received any increase. On the superannuation of Mr. M. D. Kelly, a clerk in the office of the purchasing and contract branch, the department requested the Civil Service Commissioners to advertise the vacancy. Having regard to the special qualifications required for the duties of the position, they recommended Mr. Vaughan, and his appointment was authorized by Order in Council.
Those are the only appointments in the Marine and Fisheries Department made under section 21 since I became minister of that department. I have not here a list of the appointments in the Department of Naval service, but when the Naval Service Estimates are up, I will make a statement to the House covering those appointments

I have a very strong
complaint from Mr. Kendall at Port Al-berni, B.C. Section 5 of the special Fishery Regulations for British Columbia provides that:
The Chief Inspector of Fisheries for the province is hereby empowered to cancel a fishery license forthwith for a violation of the regulations or conditions of the license by the licensee or by his representative who may be operating under such license for him.
That is a very drastic provision; it places the licensee entirely in the hand-s pf the Chief Inspector of Fisheries for the province. I am informed that there is no such provision in the Nova Scotia Fishery Regulations. I recognize that the chief inspector should have pretty large powers, but there ought to be some provision whereby proceedings might be stayed so that an appeal could be taken to the deputy minister at Ottawa. I am told that the chief inspector in British Columbia in the district in which Mr. Kendall's operations are carried on seems to have a spite against that gentleman and is acting vea-y arbitrarily, and Mr. Kendall complains very bitterly. The most I can do is to ask the minister to look into the matter, and also if he does not think there should be some provision for staying proceedings so that an appeal may be made, if it is thought desirable to make one. Otherwise, an inspector who might be so disposed, might ruin a licensee.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This case has bedn before
me off and on for a number of years, it has been reported on not only by Mr. Cunningham, our chief fishery officer in British Columbia, who is an old and experienced official, but by our fishery officers here. I shall be glad to show the hon. member the whole correspondence, and perhaps he will then be satisfied that it was impossible to take any other action than has been taken hy the department.
Will the minister sh.ow the papers to Senator Bostook who is familiar with this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have asked Mr. Found
to make a note of the matter, and I shall he glad to send the file of papers to Senator Bostock so that he may look into it himself.
Has there been any increase in the number of fishery officers in Nova Scotia during the last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
Has the minister the list of fishery guardians for the county of Richmond, N.S?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The number in the county of Richmond is twenty-six, but I have not their names here.
That is a very large increase-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is the same number as last year.
Perhaps-but a very considerable increase over the number of a few years ago. I would like a list of them. The department have been good enough to furnish me with a list in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Certainly. I have asked
Mr. Found to have a list prepared and sent to the hon. gentleman.
And may I have a similar list for the counties of Guysborough and Antigonish?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

Who compose the Advisory
Board?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There are four members
from Nova Scotia, Mr. Hemon; Mr. Short, of Digby; Captain W. C. Smith, of Lunenburg; and Mr. King, who was appointed on the recommendation of the Halifax Board of Trade. From New Brunswick, there are Mr. F. E. B. Young, of CaTaquet; Mr. Carson, of Kent County; and Mr. John Jackson, of St. John. There is also a gentleman from the Gulf District, Mr. Arsenault; and from Prince Edward Island, Mr. Long-worth, of Charlottetown.
Do they meet here?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes, together with the
officials of the department. Once they met in Nova Scotia, and once in Prince Edward Island. These gentlemen act without pay; all they receive is their actual expenses.
What are their functions ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They are purely advisory. They meet with the deputy minister, the Commissioner of Fisheries, and other officials; and discuss such matters as close seasons, fish hatcheries and other subjects relating to the fisheries, and make recommendations. The Bill which I introduced yesterday, and which was read the second time to-day and referred to the Committee on Marine and Fisheries, was prepared largely as a result of their deliberations with the officials of the department.
Mr. A'. W. CHISHOLM:	Does not the
minister realize that he has left a very large part of Nova Scotia unrepresented on the Advisory Board, in that there is no representative from Cape Breton? I regard the functions of this board as very important. It is the medium through which the fishermen can place their case before the Government. I notice that three of the Nova Scotia members of the board are from the western portion of the province, while Cape Breton, which is surrounded by the most important fishing waters of Canada, has no member on the board. I think that is a mistake, and I have called the attention of the minister to it more than once. I regret that he has not seen fit to appoint a representative from that portion of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We have requests from
time to time to appoint on the board representatives from different sections. For instance, there is no member of the board representing the county of Charlotte, N.B., though its fisheries are very important, including extensive sardine weirs and important lobster and qther fisheries. There was a representative from this section for the original board, but at his death the place was filled by the appointment of Mr. Jackson of St. John. There are other important fishing centres which are not represented on the board. We do not wish to make the board so large as to be un-

wieldy. My experience ds that you get better work from a committee if it is of reasonable size. From Nova Scotia, originally, we had only three members. Strong representations were made that, as Halifax was really the centre of the fishing trade of the Maritime Provinces, a very much larger fish trade being done there than anywhere else it was desirable that there should be a representative on the hoard from Halifax who understood the fishing tTade generally. So Mr. King, who was recommended by the Halifax board of trade, was appointed. I appreciate what the hon. member (Mr. Chisholm) says, but at the same time I think the different interests are fairly represented by those on the board. I am sure that they will see that no injustice is done to Cape Breton, and that they deal with fishery questions from the standpoint of general interest rather than from the standpoint of locality. When the hon. gentleman made his suggestion, I said 1 would consider it, and so I have, and have had considerable doubt about it; but I think it better not to have the committee too large.

What the minister (Mr. Hazen) says, concerning the county of Charlotte, applies to the locality referred to by the hon. member for Inverness (Mr. Chisholm). As the minister knows, a very large proportion of the population of Cape Breton are engaged in the fisheries. With respect to the provisions for the open and closed season for lobsters, the island of Cape Breton is to a large extent a separate district. Great difficulties have been met with by the officers of the department in their efforts to work out a scheme of open seasons for the province of Nova Scotia' suitable to the conditions and exigencies of all sections. In the spring, the fishermen of Cape Breton are handicapped by the presence of large quantities of drift ice on the coast. In some seasons the ice remains until a very late date, and the consequence is that the lobster fisheries are very much hampered as compared with other places in Nova Scotia. From time to time the fishermen of the island of Cape Breton have made special representations in favour of an extension of the open season to compensate them for the time of which they can not fish on account of the drift ice. The conditions in Cape Breton would thus seem to call for special attention on the part of the advisory board. Antigonish and Guysborough also have large fishing interests. It does seem to me that there 
should be at least one member of the board from Cape Breton and eastern Nova Scotia. The suggestion made by the hon. member for Inverness is eminently reasonable. If there was any way by which the minister could eliminate one of the present members of the Advisory Board and substitute for him a representative particularly of the island of Cape Breton, I think it would be in the public interest to do so.
Inasmuch as the minister has intimated that the members of the board do not receive any salary, and are only paid their actual expenses, it is not a position that is so remunerative that any gentleman would be loath to part with. That would make it much easier for the minister to make some change in the personnel of the board, in order that it might more directly represent the island of Cape Breton and Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The appointments are
yearly. There is a certain element of fairness in saying that the members of the board should be changed from time to time. We get fresh ideas and fresh blood and there is much force in my hon. friend's contention. What he .says about Cape Breton Island and eastern Nova Scotia is very true. The season there is later and that condition was recognized when the season in which lobsters may be caught was fixed at a later time in Cape Breton than in any other part of Nova Scotia.
That is quite true but the presence of ice on the coast makes changes necessary from time to time.

Has the Advisory Board given any advice to the minister on the urgent questions that are before him at the present time in regard to the fisheries? Members are receiving letters regarding the great scarcity of salt in order to preserve fish in the districts where they are, not doing a fresh fish business. Another question is that of the extension of the lobster season. At this season of the year members of parliament are apt to receive a good many requests of that kind and it would be interesting to know if these matters are being dealt with by the Advisory Board and if they are giving the minister advice in regard to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
By the 15th of this month we will have advice from the members of the board, and also from our officers all over the country, in regard to the desirability of making an extension if the lobster season. As the hon. gentleman knows,

I have been very loath to extend the season and I have declined to do so from jlear to year.
Never.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think that during the last three years there has been a single exception. But this year there seems to be a very persistent attempt made to secure an extension. The request comes not only from the districts which are affected but from members of the House and I have a letter from the hon. member for Guysboro pointing out reasons why he thinks there should be .an extension in certain parts of Nova Scotia. I have had representations made to me by the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Loggie) who has been a persistent advocate of not extending the season. But owing to the fact that conditions are of a most unusual character he says that . for the first time he thinks that possibly it would be in the public interest that an extension should be made. We have sometimes found that when conditions have been unfavourable at the commencement of the lobster season and fish have not been caught for a considerable time after the season opened the conditions have been so favourable during the latter part of the season that the catch has been just as good as in normal years. In view of the very strong representations that have been made to the department we have asked our fishery officers in the different districts all over the country to carefully observe and note what the catch and conditions are and to make reports to us which we will receive by the fifteenth of this month so that we will be in a position to come to an intelligent conclusion in regard to the matter. I dislike extending the seasons. They were made for the purpose of preserving the fish an,d preventing the destruction of the fisheries and it seems to me to be almost better, taking one year with another, that there should be no extension, because, while the catch might be smaller one year, perhaps as a result of the enforcement of the regulations and the preventing of the taking of a large number of lobsters, an increased catch is the result and the fishing is better in the future. However, there are other considerations which will have to be taken into account. The fishermen go to considerable expense to get their gear and supply themselves with boats and lobster traps. Some of them make it their principal source of livelihood and if they are not allowed to pursue their calling, and they get a smaller Quantity of fish, it makes the conditions
very difficult for them and that is especially the case this year when there is such a demand for food products. We have taken steps to get preliminary information to enable us to come to a wise and sound conclusion in regard to the matter.
Could the minister tell me what the dates are when the season closes on the different sections of the coastf

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It closes in different districts at different times. In the district in which the hon. member for Northumberland is interested, it closes on June 25, and in the district in which my hon. friend from Guysborough is interested, it closes on June 20. I think it is five days earlier in that part of Nova Scotia than it is along the gulf of St. Lawrence and the Northumberland Straits. It opens earlier and closes earlier in the districts on the south shore of Nova Scotia, on the bay of Fundy and in the counties of St. John and Charlotte. These dates5 of course, were fixed in consequence of the reports of commissions. There have been from time to time lobster commissions. There was one about 1897, or 1898, and in 1912 there was another to consider altered conditions. The close seasons were fixed very largely on the reports of these commissions which have been made after taking evidence and getting the views of the men who are interested in the lobster fishery on different parts of the coast of the Maritime Provinces.

I want to point out the importance of arriving at a decision as early as possible, because, if it is left until the 15th of the present month and the season closes on the 20th, there will scarcely be time enough for the fishermen to get the news on the coast. It takes several days to have them notified in regard to an extension, and if an extension is going to be made, a decision should be arrived at as soon as possible, and the fishermen given notice at least a week ahead so as to permit them to make their plans as to the . date at which they will take up their traps. With reference to the district in which I am particularly interested, from Halifax Harbour to Point Michaud, I would ask the minister to instruct the officers to telegraph the information so that the fishermen will have sufficient notice.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend's point is well taken, and we will wire if it has not already been done. When I was speaking about getting these reports on the 15th I

had mostly reference to the district where the season closes on the 25th. The commissioner tells me that we will have the report from the district in which my hon. friend is particularly interested by the 10th or 12th, and as there is very nearly a week before the close season, we will be prepared to make an announcement as to whether we shall make an extension or not.
Has the minister given any attention to the remarks I made the other day?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In regard to fishing in October?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not been able to give much attention to that question since my hon. friend made the suggestion, although it has been made before. I intend to give attention to it and to get a report on the subject. But I think the best opinion of our fishery officers is that such a course, if it were adopted, would result in the destruction of the lobsters and cause great injury to the fishery in the future. I will get all the information I can on the subject.

I hope the minister will, because I am not of opinion that fishing in the- fall would be more disastrous to the lobster industry than in the spring. I 'believe that this opinion will be supported by the fishermen on the coast. I see that the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Loggie) has been coming to my way of thinking during the past year or two, and that alone says something.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is hard not to come your way.

This question would not be complete if I did not put in a word for the coast of Quebec. The season is very late there always, starting from the mouth of the Restigouche river, they cannot place lobster traps until the end of May. So the early part of the season is lost, and they have to stop fishing when they have only properly started to work. This spring the season is much later than usual. The spring is fully a month later in Quebec, and so I hope the minister will consider that district when he is considering these points in the Maritime Provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The district to which my hon. friend refers, I presume, is up at the head of the Baie de Chaleur.
The whole coast of Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is not a very large catch. The season is late and the result is that the fishermen do not have a very long time in which to catch lobsters. But the information we have is that if you extend the season there beyond the present date the lobsters are getting in a condition when they are not fit to catch. If you catch them then you destroy them without getting very much in food value in return.

Why not give a season in the fall, as has been suggested by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon)? This is an unusual year, food supplies are very scarce, and a trial might be made this year to see the effect of a fall fishing season.

How does the minister square his statement that lobsters would not be in good condition after the 25th of June with the fact that in another district he starts the season on the 24th of May and allows it to run until the 10th of August? Does he mean that the lobsters canned in that district are not suitable for food?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I can only see that it is a bad season, but under the conditions in that district if you did not let them fish at that season you could not let them fish at all. The whole subject is a
5 p.m. most difficult one and it is hard to get fishermen to agree among themselves upon it. It is just the same with the lobster hatcheries, some of which were established before I came into office. We had been hoping that the lobster hatcheries would increase the supply of lobsters, but, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Copp) the other evening, Professor Knight, after carrying out experiments in connection with the lobster industry, is of opinion that the lobster hatcheries are not only not assisting in increasing the number of lobsters but are a detriment, because you take the female lobster and take the berries from it to send to the hatchery and then the female lobster is sent to the cannery. He has a theory that you could replenish the lobster fishing much more quickly by passing a regulation to the effect that if any female lobsters in the berry stage are caught they should at once be returned to the sea so that the increase would come about in the natural way. Dr. Knight is carrying on a very extensive inquiry in regard to this matter, and among the other subjects he has to consider is the question raised by the hon. member for Gloucester as to whether it

would not be better to prohibit entirely the catching of lobsters during the months of June, July and August, and allow fishing to take place at a later date. That is absolutely contrary to the views that have prevailed among fishery experts and officers in the past.
Where is Dr. Knight making his observations?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Dr. Knight is a professor at Queen's college, Kingston. He has been making observations at the biological station at St. Andrews, New Brunswick, at Digby, where lobsters are impounded for observation, and at points along the Nova Scotia coast and Northumberland straits. Last year he was on the Digby coast.

It should not be difficult for scientific men to be certain whether or not the lobster hatcheries are doing good work. We all know what they do. The berries are put in the jars in the hatchery and after they are hatched the little lobster is syphoned out into the sea about three miles from the coast, and we know nothing more about it. The theory %ve used to get from the scientists was that the little lobster drifted on the surface of the water for several days until his claws formed, and then he sank to the bottom and grew up to be a lobster. That is what we were told. I do not see that there can be any great trouble in ascertaining whether that is true or not It could be done by actual experiment. It should not be difficult to follow \these fry up after they are placed in the water and to ascertain from day to day whether they are still floating on the surface, or are living, or what becomes of them. It is only by actual contact with the lobster hatcheries and fisheries that the scientists can obtain proper knowledge. I think that the scientists should go to the hatchery and stay there and see how these fry get along whether they really do grow up or not. This is a matter of very great importance, as we are spending a great deal of money in the hatching of lobsters, and if there are no results, it is better to know it. We were always of the opinion that, on the coast of Pietou county, with which district my hon. friend from Pietou is more familiar than I, that the hatchery at' Caribou was doing good work. There was no part of Nova Scotia, so far as I know, where the catch of lobster was kept up better than on the northern shore served by the hatchery at Cariboo. It was one of the earliest hatcheries on the coast of Nova Scotia, and we always had the idea that in that region the supply wae being maintained. I thin-k the hon. gentleman from Pietou will agree with me m that statement. There is no reason why there should not be similar results in other places. If the minister has a really good officer to investigate, I trust he will ascertain for certain whether the lobster fry that we put in at the sea lives, grows up. and keeps the fisheries going, as we expected them to do, when we spent all this mojjey in establishing these hatcheries.

Last summer I met Professor Knight, the gentleman who was conducting the investigation in my county, where there has been a hatchery for a number of years. I was very much impressed with his anxiety to make the investigations as effective as possible. He succeeded in interesting the fishermen of the county in the problem as to how the industry could be served to a greater degree than any man I have seen representing the department in connection with that problem in the past. At various meetings held in the district he explained the process of observation which he was carrying on, that he had been at Digby, or somewhere in that vicinity, where there had been a pond, and he was comparing the results in both places, and, in addition to watching the development of the lobster in the hatcheries, he was experimenting with the production of lobsters in an artificial pond, which he built in the vicinity. One could not help being impressed with the capacity of Dr. Knight. I think he is carrying on good wprk. He has very strong views in reference to certain matters in connection with lobster propagation and development, which, no doubt, he communicated to the department, and the balance of his judgment, as I understand, was against the continuance of the hatcheries, and rather in favour of the establishment of ponds. I think, as between the two conditions under which he experimented side by side at Caribou, that better results were obtained in one than the other. That is my recollection, but I am not speaking from definite data in the matter. The idea of a fall season was urged by a great many of the fishermen in my district. I do not pretend to speak with any particular knowledge, but this view has been entertained by the fishermen in my county.

I do not think it would be in the interests of the fishermen to do away



with the spring fishing, and substitute the autumn fishing for it. The district referred to by the hon. gentleman from Bonaven-ture, I thought, was unfairly treated by the shortening of the time. The committee who had charge of it took a certain number of days off the district, and added a recommendation that the season for the district in question should be further cut, a certain number of days after the first or second year. I think the district was unfairly treated in the circumstances, this year we have only spine three or four weeks' fishing and our product will be short, and it is possible the minister may be willing, under the present circumstances,, t<o consider that, but to my mind the season in the district should extend to the end of June instead of the 25th. Then the same number of days would be taken off as has been taken off in the other districts. Regarding the hatcheries, I suppose hon. gentlemen know that fish devour one another. On one occasion I was at a hatchery near Shippigan, and these little lobsters, about the size of mosquitoes, were coming out of the shell, and the small fish that had been pumped up from the channel were devouring these little lobsters. There is a general impression that these lobsters are emptied, as it were, into the sea, and remain on the surface, and are devoured by other fish. I am quite sure that, at certain seasons of the year, other fish, say mackerel or herring, do school very largely on the surface of the water, and, of course, they are cannibals, if I may so express myself, and they devour one another, and I am under the impression that large numbers of those little lobsters thus cast upon the sea are devoured by other fish. I have heard' as a suggested remedy that the department should place these lobsters in shallow water in the seaweed, If they put them down at low water, the tide would rise and cover them, and in that way they would be on the bottom. I mention that, because there are not many fish in the bays in the summer season. Some smelts and tommy cod frequent them but not to any great extent. I have heard it suggested that much better results would be obtained if these lobsters were deposited in shallow water, in the eel grass, so that they could get to the bottom, and have time to grow and take care of themselves up to a certain time. I do not pretend to have a deep scientific knowledge along these lines, and I do not know whether that is practical or not, but I do believe it would be wise to do away with the spring fishing [M. Loggie.J
season, because pilfering would go on after the close season, as it goes on after the 25th of June. The season in that district is five days too short to be fair with the other districts. If we take up our traps on the 25th June, and keep them on shore until the lobster has shed its shell, got the new shell, and got into a hardy condition so that it moves around, as it does in the course of a few weeks, perhaps it would not be unfair to let the fishermen have, say two or three weeks in the month of September: give them the month of September, or whatever time the department find the lobster is in a wholesome condition for food, and then let everybody, small and large, try to obey the law, and avoid this charge that is so rampant, that he law is not recognized, which is quite true. There" is no question whatever about the infringement of the law. Parties will get a few cans, put these lobsters in the cans at their homes, and market them. The quality is not what it ought to be, but nevertheless the lobsters are put on the market, and they find a ready sale, especially if the supply is short. I had a telegram from home yesterday saying that at present fishing is good. In a telegram that I received to-day it was suggested that an offeT which had been received for the purchase of goods should be declined, because of the probability of the supply being short. I think that for this year the minister ought to extend until July 5 the fishing season which closes on June 25. We used to have until July 10, but subsequently ten days were taken off the time. When ten days is taken off the fishing season in one district, not more should be taken off in another. I think that in the interests of all concerned, the minister ought to give these matters consideration.

The fishermen are suffering
serious handicaps in Tespect of the cost of the necessary supplies, the cost of living and the general scarcity of food. I think, therefore, that we would not be asking too much if we requested that the close season should be entirely abolished for the present year. In the part of Nova Scotia which I represent, the fishermen are not getting as much for their catch this year as formerly, the canneries stating that the transportation of lobsters is restricted by reason of the shortage of merchant shipping. Under present war conditions, it is only fair that the fishermen should be relieved to. some extent from the difficulties under which they are working, and much would be accom-

plished in this direction by allowing them a full season',, fishing of lobsters until the fall.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am afraid that if we allowed the lobster fishing to go on without provision for a close season, the result would be prejudicial to lobster fishing in future years. To he honest with my hon. friend, I do not think that his suggestion can be complied with.

In what respect would it
have a had effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: For one thing, it would reduce the market price. The quantity of lobsters obtained would be so great that they would be a drug on the market. I do not think that it is in anybody's interest that my hon. friend's suggestion should be carried out.
One of the fishery overseers in my county, Mr. Prescott, died about a year ago. Who was appointed in his place?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My recollection is that, as about 18 miles intervened between the different points which had to be especially watched by the guardian, the district was considered too large. Accordingly, the dis-was divided and one guardian appointed for each district, the salary being divided between them. I do not recollect the names; I shall be glad to send them to my hon. friend later.

Mr. Prescott's salary was only $100, and the dividing of the district would result in the men getting $50 each, which is a very small salary. My impression is that the chief duty of an officer of , this kind is to see that no refuse from the mills gets into the fishing streams. It is a fact that the sawmills dump sawdust and other refuse into the streams which flow into fishing waters. This is not prevented by a visit from the fishery officer or by the writing of a letter. If in the opinion of my hon. friend's officials, the dumping of refuse into these waters is detrimental to fishing interests, I would suggest that he pay the officers who attend to that matter a sufficient salary and clothe them with sufficient power to enable them to prevent the practice, which has not been prevented up to the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The man who gets $500 is allowed $150 for horse hire, but he gets no mileage, as some other inspectors do. His hotel bills also are paid.
His travelling allowance is larger than a good many others, and he receives also a salary of $500.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Perhaps he has a larger district.

Edward Chute gets $500, in addition to travel and outlay, $278.91. J. A. Donovan, of Ingonish, receives the princely salary of $60, but he has the consolation of having drawn $389.32 for travel and outlay, making altogether $449.32. It seems to me that the system is antiquated, and that the salaries ought to be revised. The fact that a man draws a salary of $60 a year and receives an amount by way of travel and outlay of $389.32, indicates either that he is not getting a sufficient salary, or that he is drawing too much for travel and outlay, having regard to the work that he is doing. A few years ago all fishery officers throughout Nova Scotia were getting practically the same salary. In the last few years, however, I find that the salaries of some of these officials have advanced in a very marked degree. I do not understand that that is altogether because of any special difference in the character of the work they are doing. If the work of Mr. Donovan, for instance, of Ingonish, is such that the necessary travel and outlay should amount to $389.32, then he is entitled to a salary of more than $60 per year. The whole thing appears to be wrong; there ought to be a scale of salaries prevailing throughout Nova Scotia for all officers of that particular class. I cannot see why one fishery overseer should receive a salary of $500 and travelling expenses of $248.58, whereas another gentleman occupying the same position and doing the same work receives a salary of only $60. I do not know whether this inequality is due to influence that certain officers may have with the department as against others, but it is almost scandalous to have it appear in the public records of this country that men occupying the same positions and discharging the same duties should be compensated so unfairly and with such a great inequality.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am not disposed to differ very much from my hon. friend. There is need for a very great reorganization in connection with the salaries paid to these fishery officers. We have been able to effect that reorganization up to the present time in the western part of Nova Scotia, where we have fewer officers than we have in other parts of that province, with the result that we give them larger territory to look after and greater recompense for their services. The same question will have to be grappled with in the other parts of Nova Scotia, but 'at the present time and in the past there has been such a large number of offices that the officers have been receiving small salaries. It would be better to have fewer officers and to give them larger salaries. I hope, if we live long enough, we shall have a reorganization throughout the whole province. Some of these officers are paid small amounts such as $20 or $25, and in this day and generation you cannot expect any service of value for remuneration of that sort.
I see by the Auditor General's Report that Mr. Robert Prescott, an overseer at Baie Verte, in New Brunswick, is receiving a salary of $150, with travelling expenses of $718.29.
The $150 is put at the wrong end.

I understand that the area is a large one, and as Mr. Prescott lives inland at some distance from the shore where the factories are, he receives so much per mile for travelling expenses. I am making only the same criticism as my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte). From the Auditor General's Report I find that the expenditure in connection with the fishery overseers in the province of New Brunswick amounts to $7,195.69, hut under the heading of special guardians there is an expenditure for wages and disbursements up to March 31, 1916, of $34,429.81. There are no items or explanations with regard to this, and I would like to know what it means.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

That is all published in the official report, and I will get the information for my hon. friend.

As regards the question asked by -the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Copp), Mr. Prescott is one of the regular fishery overseers and, like all the rest, where he owns a horse himself, he is allowed ten cents a mile for the distance he travels on business connected with his position. 11 wish to draw the attention of the minister to a matter of hardship that is taking place under the administration of the department in connection with the fisheries at Lac la Biche, north of Edmonton. The minister is, of course, aware that in northern Alberta there are a. number of important lakes which furnish white fish in large quantities, and that since the recent construction of railroads, those fish are available for the world market. The question of fishing in this lake has become a commercial matter and means the investment of considerable capital. Since the railroad was constructed to Lac la Biche, there was commercial fishing for export last year. This commercial fishing is done in this way. Certain companies establish the necessary plants of houses, ice-storing, box-making and so on, and either they provide small boats and rig-outs for actual fishermen, or fishermen come in and supply their own and, sell their fish to these com=

mercial establishments which box, cool and ship the fish to the market. The buildings must be erected; the ice must be put up in the winter time, and every preparation made in advance of the actual fishing season. During the season the company depends on the fishing operations for the realization on the capital invested.
The spring fishing season opened on 5th May this year. On the day before, after all preparations had been made, all licenses issued, buildings erected, boats and nets provided, and everything else made ready, the Department of Fisheries at Ottawa wired restricting the total catch from the lake to
240,000	pounds for the season. Already the department had issued licenses for commercial fishing in the lake to the number of 125, which was 55 more than last year. By the issue of these licenses they have attracted to the lake poor men-these fishermen are generally poor-and have been the means of causing them to spend their time and invest in boats and other fishing gear, and, by issuing one-third more licenses this year than last, have led everyone to suppose that there would be no limit on the fishing; and then a wire is sent out the day before the season opens telling the licensees

Now, we are quite agreeable that the department should decide that not more than so many pounds of fish shall be taken put of the lake during the season, if they make the decision upon information and knowledge. But when they make that decision, they should not issue an unlimited number of fishing licenses, thereby inducing the investment of time and money in an enterprise that, by reason of the restriction of the department itself, cannot possibly result in advantage to the parties concerned. It may be that the Government think it does not make any difference, that it does not concern them; that they are protecting the fish and it does not matter about the people. In my judgment, it matters a great deal more about the people than about the fish. The Government has no right to deal with the people, even if they are poor people, in that way. They should exercise reasonable judgment in issuing licenses for fishing in any lake in which they intend to restrict the catch. Last year, there was no restriction on the catch, and all the fishing companies were allowed to catch as much as they could. People had no Teason to believe that there would be any restriction this year, until after every investment had
been made, and every preparation completed. If I speak strongly on tbis matter, it is because what took place in this case this year took place in the' case of Lesser Slave lake last year. In the previous season, there was unrestricted fishing in that lake, and when the next season came, after licenses had been issued, a restriction was announced. It was an unjustifiable hardship, both upon the people who are investing their money as fish exporters and upon the unfortunate fishermen who gather there. I have not heard from Lesser Slave lake this year, and I do not know the conditions there, but I do know that last year there was an unjustifiable hardship. Representations were made to the department on the subject last yeaT, and I ami astonished to know that exactly the same course has been followed in the case of Lac la Biehe this year. I cannot imagine that the minister could have had knowledge of the facts in time or it would not have occurred. I may say that the equipment of the individual fishermen costs 560 or $70, exclusive of boats, licenses, and incidentals, and the total catch allowed, if divided equally among the licenses, will not afford a return foT the' investment

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This matter was brought
to my attention on several occasions last year. Lao la Biohe, which is not a very large lake, was, until the last Jew years, so far removed from settlement that there was very little desire tp fish in it. We communicated with our inspector on the subject. The inspector visited the lake and reported that in his opinion it was not safe to allow more than

I do not wish to unduly press the department about restricting the amount of fish that may be taken from the lake and I appreciate that there may be some difficulties in adjusting the issuing of licenses. The department might take the view that it has information before it as to whether people could make a living out of fishing or not. If they choose to put it that way, that is a matter for their consideration, but what I desire to emphasize is that if they are going to restrict the amount that may be taken, and if they are not going to restrict the number of licenses to be issued, the public should have notice before they apply, that the licenses are issued subject to a restriction upon the taking of fish. With regard to Lac La Biche, my information is that licenses were issued without restriction and that preparation was made, both by the fishermen and the fish companies, tor taking an unrestricted amount of fish, but that on the 4th day of May, just before the fishing opened, they were notified not that 400,000 pounds, but that only 240,000 pounds, might be taken. I am sure that the minister must appreciate the unfortunate position that resulted from that lack of notice, The people who had obtained licenses had no means

of protecting themselves. If they had had information when they applied for licenses that the limit had to be placed on the amount of 'fish to be taken they- could have used their own judgment with regard to the matter. My information is that the people were given to understand, by reason of the action during the previous year, that they had an unrestricted right to take fish as there was no restriction on the number of licenses and it was not until every preparation was made that they were notified of this limitation and then apparently they were notified as to an amount below the mark that has finally been conceded by the department. They were notified that the amount was 240,000 pounds which was a very severe blow to their expectations. These expectations were justified in view of the policy of the department *with regard to lac la Biche last year. If a change was going to be made they should have had due notice. They did not have notice. That is exactly what occurred with regard to Slave lake a yeaT ago. I am consuming the time of the House now for the purpose of impressing upon the minister the absolute injustice of withholding this notice until such a late date, and whatever decision the department arrives at as to the amount of fish that may be taken ought to be made known from year to year before the licenses are issued, if the department does not see fit to restrict the number of licenses.

Since the House rose at six o'clock, I have been making some further investigations as to the differences in salaries of fishery overseers in the province of Nova Scotia, and these investigations confirm me in the belief that the increases that have been accorded to certain fishery overseers must have more relation to the activities of certain hon. members in this House who have the ear of the minister, than to the circumstances in which these overseers are situated or the amount of work they do. Take the salary of William Aymar, of Meteghan, in the constituency of Digby, who receives $500 a year; while Sylvester Boudrot, of Petit de Grat, in the constituency of Richmond, has to be content with a salary of $100. Edward -Chute,

of Canada Creek, in the county of Annapolis, enjoys $500; while M. J. Coady, of Southwest Margaree, in the constituency represented by my hon. friend from Inverness, has a salary of $60 only. Mr. J. G. D'Entremont, of Middle West Pubnico, fishery officer in Digby -county, enjoys $800, while J. A. Donovan, of Ingonish, in the constituency of Cape Breton North and Victoria, has to be content with $60. Mr. J. A. Evans, of Chester, in the constituency of Lunenburg, enjoys $700; while N. Ferguson, of Port Moren, South Cape Breton, receives only $55. W. E. Fraser, of Liverpool, in the county of Queens, enjoys $750; while Ed. Hall, Main-a-Dieu, South Cape Breton, has a salary of only $55. D. L. McDonald, Bailey's Brook, in the county of Pictou, is paid for his services $75; Walter Purdy, Deep Brook, $700; J. J.-Ross, North East Margaree, $60; C. F. Rathbun, Hortonville, $400 (that is in King's County, Nova Scotia, I think); T. Sullivan, Little Bras d'Or, $55; George Walls, Shelburne, $750; E. J. Thibeau, Thibeauville, in the county of Richmond, $100; R. Sutherland, River John, $150.
Hon. members of this committee will observe that in every case the fishery officers enjoying large salaries happen to reside in the counties of Nova Scotia represented by Conservative members, whereas in nearly every case the fishery overseers who must be content with a smaller salary happen to be discharging their duties in the counties of Nova Scotia represented by Liberal members.

What is the salary of the fishery officer in the county of Yarmouth?
Mr. IvYTE: Mr. D'Entremont gets a salary of $800.

The hon.
gentleman said he was in the county of Digby?
It should be Yarmouth.
Represented by a Liberal?

Unfortunately not represented at the present time, but it was represented by a Liberal. H scarcely imagine that the fishery officers who are residing in the counties represented by Conservatives have any more important duties to perform than the fishery officers in other parts of Nova Scotia. It is well known that Guysborough, Richmond, Inverness, Cape Breton are fishing counties, having a 
large portion of the population engaged in the fishing industry. The duties of inspectors in these counties are as important and the districts quite as large and as difficult to get over as in the other counties. I am not going to say at the present time that any of these gentlemen who enjoy the larger salaries are paid too much for their services, but if they are not paid too much, then the other' fishery overseers whose names I have mentioned are not receiving a sufficient salary. I am aware that before the late Government went out of office the Fisheries Department and the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries had in contemplation the readjustment of the salaries of the officers I have mentioned. Nothing effective was d6ne in that direction, and I regret very much that during the past five years the present minister has been unable to devise some plan whereby a more equitable adjustment of the salaries could be made and the grounds of complaint-and there are substantial grounds of complaint made by the fishery officers who are paid small salaries -removed. The salaries of fishery officers in the county of Richmond are: Mr. S. Boudrot, Petit de Grat, $100; Mr. Anthony Sampson, L'Ardoise, $125 ; Mr. Thibeau, $100. Probably a larger portion of the population of Richmond is engaged in fishing than in any other county in Nova Scotia. The work that is expected of the fishery officers of the county of Richmond, whose names I have just mentioned, is quite as important and exacting as , the work that pertains to the offices of gentlemen occupying similar positions throughout Nova Scotia. If those who are enjoying a salary of $600, $700 or $800 are not paid top much for their services, then certainly the officers in my county are not paid sufficient salary. The discrepancy is entirely too great. I have to congratulate my hon. friends representing Lunenberg, Shelburn, Queens, Digby and Annapolis upon their ability to impress upon the Minister <of Marine and Fisheries the necessity for securing larger salaries for the men discharging those duties in their respective constituencies. I find no fault with them whatever. I regret that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries has not been able, during the five years that he has been head of the department, to readjust the salaries so that the other fishery officers, whose names I have mentioned, would enjoy a salary adequate to the services which they perform. I am very glad to hear from the minister that the Government is contemplating a readjustment of the scale of salar-

ies, and I trust he will find himself able, during the present session of Parliament, to give some increase to the fishery officers tp whom I have referred, who aTe in receipt of small salaries. No possible defence can be made that will adequately explain the discrepancies in the salaries which I have quoted to this committee, and if a more equitable adjustment of the salaries were made, I am sure it would give satisfaction to all those who are interested in the fishing industry. -

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
As I stated this afternoon,
I am disposed very largely to agree with what my hon. friend says, and I have no hesitation in saying that there should be a reorganization and a readjustment of these salaries in a very considerable portion of Nova S-cotia. We have been able to get that Organization effected at the present time in the western counties of Nova Scotia. The result is that the number of fishery officers has been very greatly reduced in the western counties, and those who remain are given larger districts, and paid better salaries than previously. In Annapolis county there is one fishery officer, in Digby county, two, Kings county, two; Lunenburg county, two; Queen county, two; Shelburne, two; and Yarmouth, one. Those gentlemen are all receiving salaries that are fairly reasonable. They are not too large, and in addition to their salaries, instead of being allowed a mileage rate for the number of miles they travel in making their tours of inspection, they are allowed $150 for horse hire, where they keep horses themselves. Coming down to the other end of Nova Scotia, in which my hon. friend is specially interested, I find there are in Cape Breton, eight fishery officers, and these fishery officers receive small salaries, running from $55 to $155, but in addition to that they are allowed ten cents a mile travelling allowance going from one place to another. Henry A. King, Little Bras d'Or, Edward Hall, Main-a-dieu, Angus McLean, Clarks Boads, Cape Breton; J. M. Gillis, Grand Mira, Allan McDonald, Ga-barus Lake; Murdoch McLean, Leitches' Creek, Norman Ferguson, Port Morien; William Burke, Mira Ferry. In Inverness county there are six fishery officers; in Victoria county, seven.

speechtext:

speechtext:

speechtext: Under the reorganization effected in western Nova Scotia, the fishery officers are allowed $150 for the keep of their horses. In Cape Breton and the other counties the officers get a mileage allowance of 10 cents a mile.

The travelling expenses of the fishery officers in the island of Cape

Breton who are receiving salaries of from $50 to $100 are no greater than those of the fishery officers in western Nova Scotia who receive salaries as high as $500 and $700. Mr. Aymer, of Meteghan, whose salary is $500, received $248.58 for travel and outlay, whereas Mr. Thibeau of Richmond county, who gets a salary of $100, expended for travel and outlay only $212.21. Edward Chute, of Canada Creek, whose salary is $500, expended for travel and outlay $278.91, while Anthony Sampson, of L'Ar-doise, whose salary is $125, expended for travel and outlay $239.45. The minister must be mistaken when he says that the fishery officers of Cape Breton are getting more for travel and outlay than the fishery officers of western Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In the county of Cape Breton, where there are eight officers, the travelling allowances are about equal to those of the two officers in any one of the counties in western Nova Scotia. I do not think that the services in the former case are as effective, because if a man gets a fair salary he devotes his attention largely to the duties of the position, but he gets only a trifling salary of from $50 to $150 he regards the work as a kind of side-line and does not give it the attention that he otherwise would. I think it would be far better to reduce the number of officers in Cape Breton and pay adequate salaries to those who do perform the duties, as we do in western Nova Scotia. I do not say that the condition of affairs in Cape Breton is satisfactory; there must be a reorganization there as well.

The county of Cape Breton has a much larger area and a much longer coast line than any of the counties in western Nova Scotia. It necessarily follows that more officers are required there. But the gross amount paid to the eight officers in the county of Cape Breton by way of salaries is very much less than the amount paid the two officers in the county of Digby. The same applies to all the counties in the island of Cape Breton. The total amount paid for salaries and allowances of officers in the county of Cape Breton is less than that paid the smaller number of officers in any of the counties in western Nova Scotia. Either the officers in western Nova Scotia are too well paid, or those in eastern Nova Scotia are not sufficiently paid.

The hon. member for Digby the other day made a proper statement of the present business methods of the Fisheries Department. This afternoon I cited 
a case where a fishery overseer or warden in New Brunswick, whose salary is $150 a year, received last year for travel and outlay, $718.20. The minister accounted for the amount of the travel and outlay by the fact that the overseers are given a travelling allowance of 10 cents a mile. The fishery overseer to whom I referred has certain duties in connection with the lobster fisheries, the open season for the district affected being from May 24 or 25 to August 10. I am not finding fault with this man or the amount that he is paid, but I contend that it is unbusinesslike to allow a man to be his own judge in the matter of the amount of travelling that he does, for which he receives 10 cents a mile.
I contend that Mr. Morrison, the inspector of the district which comprises five counties, who is paid a salary of $2,000 a year and who has received six or seven hundred dollars for travelling expenses, should organize those counties on a business basis, finding out what would be a reasonable remuneration for the overseers and paying them that amount. This is a matter of vital importance to the people. The same thing is true throughout the whole of New Brunswick, and I presume that the same thing exists in other provinces where fishery regulations require to be enforced. I find in the same county, within twenty miles of where Fishery Overseer Prescott lives, another overseer, Mr. Vinneau, of Barachois, who has a salary of $140 a year, and whose travel and outlay amounted to $1,008.54. Such a charge for travel and outlay is absolutely unjustifiable. I know the man and the district he has to work in. This matter should not be left in its present condition, because it is not conducive to good business or an honest expenditure of public money. I understood the minister to say that he had made a change in some portions of Nova Scotia, and I hope he will do the same in New Brunswick. I am not offering any*' criticism as to the amounts these men are paid; they should be paid a reasonable remuneration for their work, but they should be paid in. such a way that the chief inspector will have a check on this expenditure, so that he can see that they are not paid for what they do not do or for any expenses not connected with their district. I find another man in Barachois in exactly the same district, with a salary of $140 and travelling expenses of $549. This man must have practically the same area to look after. When I was at home a few days ago, a gentleman from Prince Edward Island happened to call at

my office, and he asked me to bring a certain matter to the attention of the hon. member for Kings (Mr. J. J. Hughes), who I see is not in his seat. This gentleman told me that fishermen on that island started fishing for smelts without licenses for the reason that the officers had no licenses to grant them. They did not fish before the season opened, but they fished before they received licenses; they went on fishing without licenses, and they were fined for doing so. I do not say that my information is correct, but if it be so, it only goes to prove that the business of the department is not being looked after as it should be. The hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) said the other day that the department was getting into a rut and that it was time it got out of it. I do not criticise the minister for finding the rut because the department was in that state when he took office, but there is no excuse for the minister, after five years, not getting out of that rut and placing his department on a business-like basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite
correct in saying that the system which he is condemning so forcibly to-night-and I do not say without some justification-is the same system that I found in force when I came into office, and which has been in force since Confederation; but if he says that I should have got that system out of the rut in five years, I would like to know what my hon. friend has to say about his own party who were in power for fifteen years and never got that system out of the rut. I have got it out of the rut so far as western Nova Scotia is concerned, where we have made a reorganization that is working satisfactorily. We have a reorganization effected in all the western provinces and in. British Columbia, and we hope to effect a reorganization along similar lines in other parts of Nova Scotia, in New Brunswick, in Prince Edward Island, and in a section of Quebec. With regard to Prince Edward Island it is claimed that the habit has been for the fishermen to go on fishing and take out their licenses in the middle of the fishing season or after the season is over. That is a very bad and improper system, and notices were issued by the department-with the desire to get out of the rut that the hon. member refers ' to-that these licenses would have to be taken out before the season commenced, and these notices were distributed throughout the district where the fishing takes
place. In view of that, if fishermen are allowed to continue fishing without taking out licenses, and if no attention is paid to such notices, how is one ever going to get business methods introduced or get out of the rut? In consequence of fishermen having disregarded those instructions, and having violated the law, they were in some cases brought before the Court, and where offences were proved against them, they were fined.
I have been informed that the old habit had prevailed so long that people did not think we were in earnest when we said we intended to have a better system, and in view of that, that perhaps it would be a proper act this year, when we were for the first time enforcing the conditions, to have the fines refunded, and this matter is being considered by the department. My hon. friend, however, will see how unwise it would be to allow that system to continue, instead of to put it on more businesslike lines as he himself is advocating in this House to-night. It is represented to me that the statement made by my hon. friend that these licenses could not be procured is not the case. The licenses were there.

My information was that these men could not obtain their licenses in time for the opening of the season. As my hon. friend says, they had been in the habit of starting fishing without a license, and they fished for two or three days, not with any idea of evading or infringing upon the law or regulations with regard to the fishing of smelts, but because of the licenses not being procurable. They got, the licenses two or three days later on, but informations were laid against them, and fines were imposed of $5 or $10 apiece and costs.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It was nothing of the kind; the amount they were fined was the amount of the license fee they would have had to pay in any case. Of course, there would be a certain small amount of costs.

Mr. Chairman, since the committee is now considering the salaries of certain employees of the Marine'Department, I shall take upon myself to offer a few remarks as to the electoral district of Rimouski-Matane. I have just heard my hon. friends on the other side of the House intimating that in their own constituencies the employees of the department are not as well paid as others in different parts of Nova Scotia, owing to political considerations. I shall point out to the lion. Minister of Marine that in the county of Rimouski, although

we are represented by a Conservative member, there are also public servants who are poorly paid, the more so during the present emergency brought on by the high cost of living. For instance, there is at Matane a lighthouse keeper who only gets $400 a year. He is not one of my political friend, but I think that in all fairness his salary is not high enough. A salary of $400 is hardly .sufficient to support a family at the present juncture, and that man has to attend to the lighthouse day and night. Beside the salary I have just mentioned he gets $50 a year as telegraph operator, forming a total amount of $450. Now, I will point out to the hon minister that there is in the county of Bimouski another man who is not by any means a Government employee, Mr. McWilliams, who gets $500 either from the Marine Department or the Public Works Department. 'It is a bonus which has been granted to him toy the, former Administration. That man is a telegraph .operator and Teports each vessel the same as the operator at Matane. He gets $500 from the Government merely for reporting vessels, while the other who attends to the lighthouse day in and day out and who moreover acts as telegraph operator gets only $450.
It seems to me that this is a case of discrimination and that it would be an act of justice on the part of the Marine Department to adjust the salary of the operator at Matane. I shall go further and ask that the operator at Father Point be dispensed with.

Has
not Mr. McWilliam been dismissed?

He has been dismissed
as lighthouse keeper.

What was his
salary as lighthouse keeper?
Mr. BOULAY':	He gets $1,400 I think.
In the course of May last I put the following question on the Order Paper:
Q. Has J. McWilliams, G.-N. w. telegraph agent at Father Point, any position in the Government telegraph service? If so, whait are his duties?
A. The Government telegraph has no wires on the south shore of the St. Lawrence. The work in connection with the shipping and signal service, which is mainly on that side of the river, is performed on the lines of the G.N.W. Telegraph Company, and the Government, to secure efficient service, makes an allowance towards the maintenance of the Father Point telegraph station, which is the most important one on the river. This allow-

ance is $500 a year and has been paid since 1902 to the company's agent, Mr. J. McWilliams.
I am going to continue in English, -so that my hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) cam understand better. There is another matter about the county of Bimouski to which, while I am on my feet, I desire to call the attention of the minister, and. that is the rate allowed for the pay of the board of the pilots. That rate is only twenty-five cents a meal, the same rate that has been allowed for many years past. But for the last two years at any rate, that Tate is much too low. The poor hotel-keepers ought not to be called upon to board these men at less than they pay for their provisions, even if they get nothing for their trouble. I think the Government should look into this matter and dio justice not only to the public tout also to the hotel-keepers.
Does the Government employ the pilots?
There is an agreement 'between the Government and the Pilot Board that the hoards of the pilots while at Father Point -shall he paid toy the Government.
They draw large sums of money from private corporations do they not? They serve steamer lines and get so much a day, and the Government implement jt toy a -grant of so much -for each meal.

As I understand it, the arrangement was made some years ago between the Government and the Pilot Board. The question of their salaries did mot enter into it, tout, owing to special circumstances, the Government agreed to allow them 25 cents a meal for their hoard. With the present prices of food-, unless this rate is increased, the -situation will be intolerable.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I understood the hon. -member (Mr. Bonlay), in the first -place, to complain of the salaries paid to guardians on the* river -at Matane. That is a matter he would have to ibring to the attention of the Government of the province of Quebec, because the guardians who protect the river at Matane are appointed by the provincial government and paid by them, or under arrangement with the local government, by the lessees of the river. Begard-ing the matter at Father Point, to which he refers, this, of course, affects the Marine Department. The Estimates of that department were passed the other evening. I am sorry that the hon. gentleman did not bring this matter forward then,

because the Deputy Minister of Marine was present, and more definite information could have been given than I am able to give at this time. I understand that an arrangement was made by which Mr. McWilliams, telegraph operator, is paid ?400 a year for supplying certain information of value to the signal service and for information of the boats going up and down the river of value to the agents of those boats. I understand the hon. gentleman to complain, that the amount paid to Mr. McWilliams is in excess of the amount paid to an officer elsewhere. I will look into the matter to see if there is any discrepancy and whether the allowance made to the operator at the other point rhould be brought up to that paid to Mr. McWilliams. The hon. gentleman also referred to the allowance made for hoard of the pilots. My attention was called to this matter for the first time few days ago. It was represented to me that years ago an agreement was made that the pilots that go to Father Point, and wait there to take vessels up the St. Lawrence from the sea, were allowed 25 cents a meal. It was represented that, in view of the high cost of living, this rate was not sufficient, and that it ought to be increased to 40 cents a meal. I instructed the officials to look up the file and get the facts, so that I could look into the matter and see just what the liability of Parliament was. As soon as I get the facts I shall be prepared to deal with the case.

I have listened to the
hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Boulay) with some regret. I thought he had forgotten his recent quarrels with Mr. McWilliams. I regret that Mr. McWilliams was dismissed as lighthouse keeper some years ago, but, of course, the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr, Hazen) had to yield to the pressure which was put upon him. I do npt know whether it may have been Mr. McWilliams' Sins of omission or commission, but let it be said that the Shipping Federation has stood by Mr. McWilliams' from the very beginning. He is a man of great ability and one who thoroughly knows his business. He has fortunately 'been kept as the telegraph operator. It is admitted amongst those who know him in the province, and particularly amongst the business men, that he is pne of the ablest operators in Canada. It is really a pity that Mr. McWilliams was dismissed and that he lost such a good income as .the one he had when he was lighthouse keeper. He is highly respected by
the business community. He was one of the few English-speaking employees of the Government in the whole district pf Quebec. I repeat that it is a pity
9 p.m. that such a man was dismissed from office but fortunately the minister did not yield to the pressure put upon him to dismiss him as telegraph operator. If my hon. friend from Rimouski will accept the opinion of such men as Lord Shaughnessy, or the president of the Shipping Federation in Montreal, he will know that Mr. McWilliams is one pf the safest, one of the ablest, men they had in the service. I think my hon. friend ought now to insist that Mr. McWilliams be restored to his former position. I know that he had some petty quarrels with him but after all a man is a man and in times like the present we pught to forget these old feuds. I regret exceedingly that Mr. McWilliams' salary has been curtailed to the extent that it has and my hon. friend should do an act of justice, be a man, and have him restored to his former position.

I am rather surprised that the hon. member for Rou-ville (Mr. Lemieux) should attempt to vindicate the worst case of political partisanship extant in the county of Rimouski and Matane. If ever public officer was rightfully dismissed, Mr. McWilliams is the man. He was for a period of thirty-six years in the service of the Government and he acknowledged to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that he had been an active political worker against the Conservative party during that period. I believe the Liberal party would not have been slow in dismissing him had he worked against them.
A fault confessed is half pardoned.
The Liberal party has never been very much in the habit of pardoning, and I do not think he would have been pardoned under such conditions.
It is never too late to reform.

I may say. to the hon.member for Rouville that should he wish to vindicate political partisanship, he might surely select a better case; Mr. McWilliams' case is the worst to be found not only in the county of Rimouski, but throughout the province of Quebec.
